newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK BONDS TO RALLY ON TIGHTER ECON POLICY - BOFA.
newsitem.headline: GREEK BONDS TO RALLY ON TIGHTER ECON POLICY - BOFA.

text.p: Greek bonds are likely to rally if the new government to be elected on September 22 takes bold fiscal measures in November but the risk-reward profile of long drachma forex positions appears no longer attractive, said Bank of America.

"Whereas bond prices could suffer short-term, the right conditions for a rally could be in place, if a bold fiscal package is presented in November," said Bank of America Global Capital Markets in its "Bond strategy - Italy, Spain and Greece," September-October issue.

Demand for T-bills will remain anemic as ex-post real yields are pushed down and spreads over the marker 12-month T-bill on seven-year floaters may narrow by 25 to 50 basis points as the new government of either major party has little option but to take strong fiscal and incomes policy measures.
The 12-month T-bill is forecast to drop to 11.50 percent by end-1996 from 12.80 percent in early August.

The rewarding long drachma, short ecu trades in 1996 which offered a double gain from interest rate differentials and the small spot appreciation of the drachma versus the ecu will no longer be attractive in 1997, the report said.
The deterioration of the country's external position will likely lead the authorities to a faster slide of the drachma until end-1996 and 1997, implying a depreciation of at least 4.5 percent.
This will negate most of the expected interest rate differential, it said.

The report said that a one-shot correction of the cumulative overvaluation of the drachma, estimated at 15 to 20 percent, remains unlikely but the risk of such an eventuality increases with a major fiscal tightening package for 1997 and a continued sharp deterioration in the current account.

The 1996 current account deficit is projected to rise to 3.3 percent of GDP with more than half being the outcome of strong imports of capital goods, higher foreign debt servicing and slower tourist inflows.
The current account deficit was forecasted at 2.1 percent of GDP in 1995, it said.
The remainder of the deterioration seems to be linked to the cumulative overvaluation of the drachma that has hit Greek export services.

"Further planned real appreciation of the drachma into 1997 is now tacitly opposed by the authorities. The recent changes at the top leadership of the Bank of Greece tend to confirm this policy adjustment," it said.
Nickos Garganas was appointed new deputy governor at the central bank replacing Evangelos Kourakos in July.

Inflation has found a tough floor at eight percent and more significant progress without a tighter fiscal, incomes policy mix no longer appears possible. The hard drachma policy seems to have reached its limits, said Bank of America.
